In [[probability theory]] and [[statistics]], the '''Conway–Maxwell–binomial (CMB)''' distribution is a three parameter discrete probability distribution that generalises the [[binomial distribution]] in an analogous manner to the way that the [[Conway–Maxwell–Poisson distribution]] generalises the [[Poisson distribution]].  The CMB distribution can be used to model both positive and negative association among the [[Bernoulli distribution|Bernoulli]] summands,.<ref name=S05/><ref name=Kadane16/>

The [[distribution (mathematics)|distribution]] was introduced by Shumeli et al. (2005),<ref name=S05>Shmueli G., Minka T., Kadane J.B., Borle S., and Boatwright, P.B. "A useful distribution for fitting discrete data: revival of the Conway–Maxwell–Poisson distribution." [[Journal of the Royal Statistical Society]]: Series C (Applied Statistics) 54.1 (2005): 127–142.[https://dx.doi.org/10.1111/j.1467-9876.2005.00474.x]</ref> and the name Conway–Maxwell–binomial distribution was introduced independently by Kadane (2016) <ref name=Kadane16>Kadane, J.B. " Sums of Possibly Associated Bernoulli Variables: The Conway–Maxwell–Binomial Distribution." Bayesian Analysis 11 (2016): 403–420.</ref> and Daly and Gaunt (2016).<ref name=DG16>Daly, F. and Gaunt, R.E. " The Conway–Maxwell–Poisson distribution: distributional theory and approximation." ALEA Latin American Journal of Probabability and Mathematical Statistics 13 (2016): 635–658.</ref>

== Probability mass function ==

The Conway–Maxwell–binomial (CMB) distribution has [[probability mass function]]

:<math>
\Pr(Y=j)=\frac{1}{C_{n,p,\nu}}\binom{n}{j}^\nu p^j(1-p)^{n-j}\,,\qquad j\in\{0,1,\ldots,n\},
</math>

where <math>n\in\mathbb{N}=\{1,2,\ldots\}</math>, <math>0\leq p\leq1</math> and <math>-\infty<\nu<\infty</math>.  The [[normalizing constant]] <math>C_{n,p,\nu}</math> is defined by

:<math>
C_{n,p,\nu}=\sum_{i=0}^n\binom{n}{i}^\nu p^i(1-p)^{n-i}.
</math>

If a [[random variable]] <math>Y</math> has the above mass function, then we write <math>Y\sim\operatorname{CMB}(n,p,\nu)</math>.

The case <math>\nu=1</math> is the usual binomial distribution <math>Y\sim\operatorname{Bin}(n,p)</math>.

== Relation to Conway–Maxwell–Poisson distribution ==

The following relationship between Conway–Maxwell–Poisson (CMP) and CMB random variables <ref name=S05/> generalises a well-known result concerning Poisson and binomial random variables.  If <math>X_1\sim \operatorname{CMP}(\lambda_1,\nu)</math> and <math>X_2\sim \operatorname{CMP}(\lambda_2,\nu)</math> are [[Dependent and independent variables#Mathematics|independent]], then <math>X_1\,|\,X_1+X_2=n\sim\operatorname{CMB}(n,\lambda_1/(\lambda_1+\lambda_2),\nu)</math>.

== Sum of possibly associated Bernoulli random variables ==

The random variable <math>Y\sim\operatorname{CMB}(n,p,\nu)</math> may be written <ref name=S05/> as a sum of [[exchangeable random variables|exchangeable]] Bernoulli random variables <math>Z_1,\ldots,Z_n</math> satisfying

:<math>
\Pr(Z_1=z_1,\ldots,Z_n=z_n)=\frac{1}{C_{n,p,\nu}}\binom{n}{k}^{\nu-1}p^k(1-p)^{n-k},
</math>

where <math>k=z_1+\cdots+z_n</math>.  Note that <math>\operatorname{E}Z_1\not=p</math> in general, unless <math>\nu=1</math>.

== Generating functions ==

Let

:<math>
T(x,\nu)=\sum_{k=0}^n x^k\binom{n}{k}^\nu.
</math>

Then, the [[probability generating function]], [[moment generating function]] and [[characteristic function]] are given, respectively, by:<ref name=Kadane16/>

:<math>
G(t)=\frac{T(tp/(1-p),\nu)}{T(p(1-p),\nu)}, 
</math>
:<math>
M(t)=\frac{T(\mathrm{e}^tp/(1-p),\nu)}{T(p(1-p),\nu)}, 
</math>
:<math>
\varphi(t)=\frac{T(\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}t}p/(1-p),\nu)}{T(p(1-p),\nu)}.
</math>

== Moments ==

For general <math>\nu</math>, there do not exist closed form expressions for the [[moment (mathematics)|moment]]s of the CMB distribution. Having said that, the following mathematical relationship holds:<ref name=DG16/>

Let <math>(j)_r=j(j-1)\cdots(j-r+1)</math> denote the [[falling factorial]]. If <math>Y\sim\operatorname{CMB}(n,p,\nu)</math>, where <math>\nu>0</math>, then

:<math>
\operatorname{E}[((Y)_r)^\nu]=\frac{C_{n-r,p,\nu}}{C_{n,p,\nu}}((n)_r)^\nu p^r\,,
</math>
for <math>r=1,\ldots,n-1</math>.

== Mode ==

Let <math>Y\sim\operatorname{CMB}(n,p,\nu)</math> and define

:<math>
a=\frac{n+1}{1+\left(\frac{1-p}{p}\right)^{1/\nu}}.
</math>

Then the [[mode (statistics)|mode]] of <math>Y</math> is <math>\lfloor a\rfloor</math> if <math>a</math> is not an [[integer]].  Otherwise, the modes of <math>Y</math> are <math>a</math> and <math>a-1</math>.<ref name=DG16/>

== Stein characterisation ==

Let <math>Y\sim\operatorname{CMB}(n,p,\nu)</math>,  and suppose that <math>f:\mathbb{Z}^+\mapsto\mathbb{R}</math> is such that <math>\operatorname{E}|f(Y+1)|<\infty</math> and <math>\operatorname{E}|Y^\nu f(Y)|<\infty</math>.  Then <ref name=DG16/>

:<math>
\operatorname{E}[p(n-Y)^\nu f(Y+1)-(1-p)Y^\nu f(Y)]=0.
</math>

== Approximation by the Conway–Maxwell–Poisson distribution ==

Fix <math>\lambda>0</math> and <math>\nu>0</math> and let <math>Y_n\sim\mathrm{CMB}(n,\lambda/n^\nu,\nu)</math>  Then <math>Y_n</math> [[convergence of random variables|converges]] in distribution to the <math>\mathrm{CMP}(\lambda,\nu)</math> distribution as <math>n\rightarrow\infty</math>.<ref name=DG16/>  This result generalises the classical Poisson approximation of the binomial distribution.

== Conway–Maxwell–Poisson binomial distribution ==

Let <math>X_1,\ldots,X_n</math> be Bernoulli random variables with [[joint distribution]] given by

:<math>
\Pr(X_1=x_1,\ldots,X_n=x_n)=\frac{1}{C_n'}\binom{n}{k}^{\nu-1} \prod_{j=1}^np_j^{x_j}(1-p_j)^{1-x_j},
</math>

where <math>k=x_1+\cdots+x_n</math> and the normalizing constant <math>C_n^\prime</math> is given by

:<math>
C_n'=\sum_{k=0}^n \binom{n}{k}^{\nu-1} \sum_{A\in F_k} \prod_{i\in A} p_i \prod_{j\in A^c}(1-p_j),
</math>

where

:<math>
F_k=\left\{A\subseteq\{1,\ldots,n\}:|A|=k\right\}.
</math>

Let <math>W=X_1+\cdots+X_n</math>.  Then <math>W</math> has mass function

:<math>
\Pr(W=k)=\frac{1}{C_n'}\binom{n}{k}^{\nu-1}\sum_{A\in F_k}\prod_{i\in A}p_i\prod_{j\in A^c}(1-p_j),
</math>

for <math>k=0,1,\ldots,n</math>.  This distribution generalises the [[Poisson binomial distribution]] in a way analogous to the CMP and CMB generalisations of the Poisson and binomial distributions.   Such a random variable is therefore said <ref name=DG16/> to follow the Conway–Maxwell–Poisson binomial (CMPB) distribution.  This should not be confused with the rather unfortunate terminology Conway–Maxwell–Poisson–binomial that was used by <ref name=S05/> for the CMB distribution.

The case <math>\nu=1</math> is the usual Poisson binomial distribution and the case <math>p_1=\cdots=p_n=p</math> is the <math>\operatorname{CMB}(n,p,\nu)</math> distribution.
